Extensive Ongentoro Overanalysis

Filed under: #translation

Introduction

On May 17th, 2026, I published a Tumblr post translating and analyzing the song Ongentoro by avogado6. I've made tons of edits to the post since then, and it's garnered some positive reception. My "posts" page has been a bit empty looking so I decided to add it here. I also wanted to spread this post outside of Tumblr so all of you guys can become UTAU too.

All you need to know for this post is what UTAU is. And if you don't know: they're basically singing voice synthesizers that are entirely free, and anyone can make one. Freeware Vocaloid. There you go; we're all on the same page, now.

There are a ton of hyperlinks, and I recommend clicking them if you'd like more information about certain things. I also recommend reading all the footnotes.

I've made some edits to account for me posting this on a website instead of Tumblr, but otherwise the content is the same on Tumblr and my website (or at least, that's the goal).

Title

音源吐露 (ongentoro) is a title pun, which makes it difficult to translate. vgperson calls it "Synth Expression" on her website. "Sound Source Revealed" is what the YouTube video claims it's called in English, but I don't know about that one…

Avogado6 loves title puns (hey, I do, too; I'm a very punny guy cue laugh track). Their demo song for Calogado's first voicebank, OREMO UTAU, has a title pun. (OREMO is a program used to record UTAU voicebanks, but "OREMO UTAU" in Japanese — as 俺も歌う — means "I'll sing, too.")

A song they made with flower, へる (heru), is also a title pun (heru means to diminish but could also be "hell." Both meanings are used in the song).

オンゲントロ (ongentoro spelled in katakana; link is region-blocked) is a term that mainly prevails in the Japanese vocalsynth community. It's a youkai that utters the spell "don't you want to record a voicebank, too?" (お前も音源を録らないか？, omae mo ongen o toranai ka?)

録る (toru, to record) is inflected in both ongentoro and toranai, but it's still the same base verb. Specifically: toro is in the imperative (commanding you do something) and toranai in the negative (but before ka, it's used to be like "won't you?").

Basically, the name of the youkai is "record a voicebank!"

The title of the song is spelled with kanji that mean "voicebank" (音源, so it's the same) and expressing how one really feels (吐露, so this one is changed!).

I think Synth Expression is a good translation of the title. (Vocal)synth is a common slang term in the English Vocaloid community used to mean "voicebank;" expression is (obviously) similar to "expressing how one really feels," but it's also a term used in the UTAU program (and Vocaloid, and related software).

Unfortunately(?), there's no youkai that haunts the English Vocaloid community, but we can change that together.

Throughout this post, I'll be referring to the song as Ongentoro, because I'm very used to calling it that, to the point where I can't call it anything else.

In General

The main premise is that Calogado (voiced by avogado6) is trying to force Mayoi Heki[1] (voiced by Hasegawa Maigo) to sing so they[2] can turn him into an UTAU.

Music Video: In General

The MV is super cute and I like it a lot. It includes fun rhythm game/visual novel segments that you sadly can't play and just have to stare at forlornly.

When Ongentoro was inducted into the Vocaloid Hall of Fame, avogado6 released an Ongentoro Stalker Solo Practice Video on Niconico Douga Shorts[3] (later released on YouTube Shorts), which is still not a rhythm game because it's a video. (You can't embed NND videos so here's the upload on YouTube shorts)

Anyway, besides the point. I still like the MV, regardless of its interactivity or lack thereof. I also like how it's monochrome (sans the Stalker Solo text). In general, the visual simplicity is a extreme charm point for me.

More on the topic of video games: the music video starts with a "powering up" SFX as Calogado and Heki fly onto the screen. When Heki's calling the police, an action command shows up above him. The end of the video has a game over SFX!

I love the video game motif. The song 100% sounds like it could be from a video game, even LOL. This was most certainly intentional — Calogado finds stalking Heki just like a fun video game.

During Calogado's part of the hook, the background shows spinning folders. Folders are kinda Calogado's character item — their glasses are even in the shape of a folder!

In Heki's, the background shows spinning compasses. These are kinda Heki's character item. I find this ironic, since he's canonically bad at directions.

Also, the animation transition from the folders to the compasses (and back) is very smooth. I'm a very huge fan.

Thumbnail

I have nowhere else good to mention this. I think it's funny that Calogado's in the NicoNico Douga thumbnail but Heki's in the YouTube one.

YouTube and probably NND set like, automatic thumbnails but I wouldn't be surprised if this was intentional.

Video and Lyrics

I'm not a native Japanese speaker, but I tried my best. I've also explained some of my translation choices. I romanized everything myself.

Calogado's parts will be in green and Mayoi Heki's in blue.

声帯をぶち盗って！
人魚姫 どうか騙されて！
8モーラ 200くらいの文章で
レシピ通り作るから

seitai o buchi totte!
ningyohime douka damasarete!
hachi moora nihyaku kurai no bunshou de
reshipi doori tsukuru kara

I'm ripping out your vocal cords!
Little Mermaid, please be tricked by me!
In 8 morae and around 200 lines,
I'll make it by following the recipe

I like how every verse ends with te or de (which is just voiced te anyway) except for the last one.

声帯をぶち盗って！
seitai o buchi totte!
I'm ripping out your vocal cords!

ぶち (buchi) is a prefix that adds emphasis to a verb, making it more strong, violent, or sudden. 盗る (toru) just means to steal — and that's what I originally went with. I decided to change it to "ripping out," though, since the imagery there is much more forceful and violent.

"To steal" and "to record" are pronounced the same way in Japanese, making for a great pun. Unfortunately, I'm not sure how to make this work in English. You can "rip audio" from a video… but it's not the same.

When spelled like 取っ手, totte can mean handle, grip, or knob. Like door handle, for example. Like how Calogado's on the other side of Heki's door…!? Though, I'm not sure if this was intentional or if I'm slowly going crazy.

人魚姫 どうか騙されて！
ningyohime douka damasarete!
Little Mermaid, please be tricked by me!

The Japanese name of The Little Mermaid is 人魚姫 (ningyohime, mermaid princess). Ongentoro makes a few references to The Little Mermaid. I'll talk about both the 1989 Disney movie and the original 1837 fairy tale, though the movie, being more popular, is probably what's being referenced in particular.

In the tale, the mermaid's tongue gets cut off by the sea witch, who finds her voice incredibly beautiful. This doesn't happen to Heki (or Ariel, in the movie), but it's another reason why I chose "ripping out."

While The Little Mermaid is not about sirens, I can't help but think about sirens here. Commonly portrayed as mermaids in fiction, and meant to lure people to their death by their impossibly beautiful singing voice.

8モーラ 200くらいの文章で
hachi moora nihyaku kurai no bunshou de
In 8 morae and around 200 lines,

This is a reference to a specific reclist created by Kurosu[4] (first .txt file). Reclists, short for recording lists, are lists of all the sounds you need to record for a voicebank[5]. A mora is the shortest unit of timing, around the same time as a syllable, but importantly not a syllable.

Since there are a lot of sounds to record, reclists are broken up into lines. Kurosu's 8 morae list method has 8 morae in each line, and really moreso around 150 linesbut I guess 200 is close enough to 150. Calogado loves Kurosu's 8 morae list method.

レシピ通り作るから
reshipi doori tsukuru kara
I'll make it by following the recipe

Calogado dresses like a chef when they say this, whipping up a serving of .wav files. WAV files are one of the "ingredients" to create an UTAU; you can't have an UTAU without audio.

And the "recipe" is the steps to create an UTAU. In The Little Mermaid, there's also a recipe which the sea witch prepares. One of the ingredients to this recipe is the mermaid's tongue, to represent her voice (the movie isn't as grotesque, instead showing an abstraction of Ariel's voice).

So, we've already established something here: Calogado's the sea witch, and Heki's the mermaid. As the sea witch, Calogado wants to trick the mermaid Heki into giving up his voice.

While Ariel doesn't know Ursula is stalking her, Heki is well aware he's being stalked by Calogado. Interestingly, like Ursula, Calogado also has a mole on the right side of their face. This could mean nothing.

来ないで！
そうやって押しかけて
泥棒ね いつもなりゆきで
幾星霜 何万回の催促 除霊に来て陰陽師

konaide!
sou yatte oshikakete
dorobou ne itsumo nariyuki de
ikuseisou nanmankai no saisoku
jorei ni kite onmyouji

Go away!
Showing up out of the blue like that
You thief! I'll never change my mind
no matter how many times you come knocking.
Come and perform an exorcism, Onmyouji!

Same thing happens here with the first three verses ending in te/de, except it comes with an extra verse.

来ないで！
konaide!
Go away!

Really, this is more of "don't come," but I didn't find that forceful enough. "Don't come!" is also not something we typically exclaim in English.

泥棒ね いつもなりゆきで
dorobou ne itsumo nariyuki de
You thief! I'll never change my mind

なりゆき (nariyuki) refers to the course of events or result of something. It could also be "by chance," but I highly doubt it's being used here to mean that. It's also an abbreviation for market order, but I highly highly doubt this one.

いつもなりゆき (itsumo nariyuki) could then be like "this is always the course of events." I've chosen to translate this quite differently, though, because the literal translation is pretty vague (what ends up this way?).

The course of events refers to, probably, how Heki always rejects Calogado's advances incessant demands of "won't you record a voicebank, too?" even though Calogado's been pressing him tens of thousands of times. So, "I'll never change my mind."

幾星霜 何万回の催促
ikuseisou nanmankai no saisoku
no matter how many times you come knocking.

"Come knocking" is — as you probably know — an idiom meaning to arrive unannounced. Additionally, Calogado is literally knocking on Heki's door, so that's another reason why I went with that.

幾星霜 is a poetic way of saying "over many years." 星霜 (seisou) means "year" but it's a combination of the kanji star + frost. The idea is that "lots of stars have risen" and "lots of snow has fallen."

除霊に来て陰陽師
jorei ni kite onmyouji
Come and perform an exorcism, Onmyouji!

An onmyouji exorcises youkai (and also does other stuff), and Calogado is of course an Ongentoro youkai. (The sea witch and an Ongentoro youkai?! Can Heki catch a break?) This reading will be elaborated on in a second.

Heki even dresses like an onmyouji when he says this. Aww, how cute.

あなたもUTAUになりませんか？
私の言うことを繰り返すだけですぐにUTAUになれますよ
基本タダですよ
このデザインどうですか？
妖怪オンゲントロはいつでもあなたを狙っています！
適度に騙されましょう！

anata mo UTAU ni narimasenka?
watashi no iu koto o kurikaesu dake sugu ni UTAU ni naremasu yo
kihon tada desu yo
kono desain dou desu ka?
youkai ongentoro wa itsudemo anata o neratteimasu!
tekido ni damasaremashou!

Won't you become an UTAU, too?
Just repeat after me, and soon you'll be able to.
It's basically free.
How's this design?
The Ongentoro youkai is always after you!
Let yourself be tricked by it (but not too much)!

This whole segment is a reference to a tweet on avogado6's vocalsynth account — and more specifically, the second picture. In fact, the words (almost) are the exact same! (無料, muryou, is used there, but off to the side it's shown to be pronounced like タダ, tada. Both of these words mean "free.")

Calogado's saying the "Won't you become an UTAU, too? / … / How's this design?" part; the text below them is "The Ongentoro youkai is always after you!" and the text below that is "let yourself be tricked by it (but not too much)!" So, once again, Calogado's being portrayed as an Ongentoro youkai.

That tweet's a bit old, now. I wonder how long Ongentoro's been cooking. Has avogado6 had this idea for a year? or did they just think referencing a tweet they made was funny? Is Hasegawa Maigo the unnamed Voca-P here!? (That might be true, since Mayoi Heki was conceptualized before that tweet. In December 2025, Mayoi Heki's recording had been completed, so it took around nine months, like a pregnancy.)

I am inclined to say, honestly, that it is a possibility avogado6 was already thinking about Ongentoro even as early back as April 2025.

In the background of this part, there's some text scrolling horizontally (what I like to call "marqueeing") behind Calogado:

UTAU県警からお知らせ　
ギ○ファイル便 ・g○○gle drive・Dropb○xなどでWAV送れは詐欺です！※場合に寄ります　
勧誘に注意しましょう！

This is also taken from the tweet in question, besides the "UTAU県警からお知らせ" part, which is new!

Here's my translation:

Announcement from UTAU Prefectural police:
Sending .wav files via Gigafile-bin[6], Google Drive, Dropbox, etc., is a scam! (on a case-by-case basis)
Let's exercise caution around solicitations!

The idea of an "UTAU prefecture" is one that shows up frequently in avogado6's illustrations, like in this tweet with Nurse Robot Type T and Dr. Dareka.

If you're curious, Calogado's voice lines are: はじめまして (hajimemashite, nice to meet you), えへへ (ehehe), なんと (nanto, well…), ほーら (hoora, look), ふふふ (fufufu), おんげんとろ (ongentoro).

Technically, these aren't voice lines: they're voice barks, but whenever I search up the term "voice barks" I get like, 90% actual dog barking, so I'm assuming this is a very obscure term. We're going to keep using "voice lines," okay?

帰れ 帰れ すぐ帰れ
手元入力110

kaere kaere sugu kaere
temoto nyuuryoku hyakutooban

Leave. Leave! Leave me alone!
I'm dialing 110.

帰れ 帰れ すぐ帰れ
kaere kaere sugu kaere
Leave. Leave! Leave me alone!

すぐ帰れ (sugu kaere) might be translated more literally as "leave right now!" or "leave immediately!" but those 1. don't sound forceful enough (again) 2. don't sound like something someone would say in this situation (a bit too stiff?) 3. don't flow that good. The point of this line is that Heki's exasperated, more or less, and I think "leave me alone" captures that idea well.

手元入力110
temoto nyuuryoku hyakutooban
I'm dialing 110.

手入力 (tenyuuryoku) means "manual input" — 手 (te) means "hand," so it is as literal as you can get. However, 手元 (temoto, area around the hands) is used here instead because Heki's sleeves are too long. Initially, I was going to translate this as "I'm calling 110," but I feel "dialing" is more akin to the meaning of "manual input;" it evokes the idea of pressing numbers on a keypad.

110 (hyakutoo) is the police number in Japan, so, like, 911. I didn't want to Americanize it, so I left it alone. I was thinking about changing it to "calling the police," but I think explaining that 110 is the police number is enough.

The ban in hyakutooban is from 番, meaning "number." It's placed at the end of phone numbers (among other things).

出せ 出せ 声を出せ
音源録らせろWAVファイル

dase dase koe o dase
ongen torasero WAV fairu

Give up. Give up! Give up your voice!
And let me record it in a .wav file

出せ 出せ 声を出せ
dase dase koe o dase
Give up. Give up! Give up your voice!

出せ is really more like "open up" or "come out" than "give up." The reason I translated it to "give up" here is so it flows nicely into 声を出せ (koe o dase) — something like "Open up. Open up! Give up your voice" doesn't work as well.

The implication (I'm trying to make) is that Heki should "give up" trying to stop Calogado and let them in! Also: in The Little Mermaid, the mermaid literally gives up her voice to the sea witch.

音源録らせろWAVファイル
ongen torasero WAV fairu
And let me record it in a .wav file

As mentioned previously, Ongentoro comes from ongen + imperative of toru. The imperative (+ causative) form(s) is(are) used here in ongen torasero.

いいでしょ？
ねえ いいでしょ？
怖くないよ 皆やってるよ

ii desho?
nee ii desho?
kowakunai yo minna yatteru yo

You don't mind, right?
Hey. You don't mind, right?
Don't be scared. Everyone's doing it.

そうだな
ん－　そうだな

soudana
nn soudana
nara iika

Hmm…really?
Well, I guess it's fine, then…

良いんだね？

iin da ne?

It's fine, you said?

声帯をぶん盗られ
人魚姫 陸に揚げられて！
3の機材 8のソフトに囲まれて
待ち構える魔女の家

seitai o bun dorare
ningyohime riku ni agerarete!
san no kizai hachi no sofuto ni komarete
machikaeru majo no ie

My vocal cords are being ripped out
Little Mermaid, you've been washed ashore!
Surrounded by 3 devices and 8 software,
the witch's house lies in wait

The lyrics are fun here since they all end in e. In Japanese, the "r" and "t" sounds are close together, so they rhyme better here. This pattern is broken by the final line, again.

声帯をぶん盗られ
seitai o bun dorare
My vocal cords are being ripped out

ぶん (bun) is another way of saying ぶち. BTW: these are not synonyms, they are different versions of the same word, like "don't" vs "do not."

Here, torare is being pronounced like dorare. (This is not standard at all and never happens[7].) Along with the aforementioned bun, this makes ぶん盗られ sound like 分捕られ (being plundered/captured/seized).

It's probably just in English, but the word "plundered" sort of connects with The Little Mermaid (plunder > ship > prince was on a ship, and that's how the little mermaid meets the prince).

Below, I put a screenshot of Heki's verse (official files from the Ongentoro folder) where you can see the note is ど (do) and not と (to). I am not crazy.

3の機材 8のソフトに囲まれて
san no kizai hachi no sofuto ni komarete
Surrounded by 3 devices and 8 software,

3 devices:

  • Microphone
  • PC
  • Audio interface

8 software:

  • UTAU
  • OpenUTAU
  • OREMO
  • setParam
  • wavTar
  • frqeditor
  • iZotope RX
  • DAW

This is a list of (not all) the things used to create an UTAU/make music with an UTAU, but you don't need all of these, and there are some things you can substitute with other things (like you can replace OREMO with RecStar).

待ち構える魔女の家
machikaeru majo no ie
the witch's house lies in wait

The witch's house is of course Calogado's house. In the tale, her house is surrounded by polypi and snakes (in the movie, just polypi, along with her eels Jetsam and Flotsam). Also, her house is made out of human skeletons. So, I'm glad Calogado's is only surrounded by computer stuff.

逃げるな！
stay up 録音リスト呪文唱えて
王子様 沼で手を振って
1音階 1000くらいの設定で
すぐになめらかoverlap

nigeruna!
stay up jumon tonaete
oujisama numa de te o futte
ichi onkai sen kurai no settei de sugu ni nameraka overlap

Don't run away!
Stay up and chant the spell
My dear prince, I'm waving my hand in the mire.
With a monopitch and around 1000 settings,
I'll easily have a smooth overlap.

逃げるな！
nigeruna!
Don't run away!

In Ongentoro's description, avogado6 has a Q&A segment where they end every answer with "don't run away," almost acting as Calogado.

stay up 録音リスト呪文唱えて
stay up jumon tonaete
Stay up and chant the spell

録音リスト means "reclist," but it's pronounced like "spell" (呪文, jumon) here. Normally, this would be pronounced rokuon risuto. Reclists are kind of written like incantations or spells; avogado6 uses a reclist a bit later into the song, so you'll see what I mean there.

Instead of its typical ア (a) for avogado6, Calogado's ahoge is kinda shaped like a heart here. They're really happy!

王子様 沼で手を振って
oujisama numa de te o futte
My dear prince, I'm waving my hand in the mire.

The sea witch doesn't meet the prince in the tale, and while she does meet him in the movie (as Vanessa), he never visits her home. This is a 3 minute song that isn't even about The Little Mermaid though so this is probably fine.

沼 (numa) is closer to "marsh" than "mire," but in The Little Mermaid, the sea witch is specifically described as living in a mire. It's also slang for obsession or addiction, like how Calogado could be described as being addicted to Heki's voice (or voice synthesis in general!). Perchance.

1音階 1000くらいの設定で
ichi onkai sen kurai no settei de
With a monopitch and around 1000 settings,

UTAU synthesis programs do not automatically know where one note starts and the other ends. You have to tell it where each note name (alias) is by configuring parameters from an oto.ini file. This is called "otoing" in the anglophone UTAU sphere. A program like setParam or vLabeler is used for this; editing the oto.ini file directly is a very bad idea.

Every configuration is put on a separate line in the oto.ini, like this:

Each line is showing the .wav file name (first), the alias (second), and the parameters (third).

Calogado's voicebank has around 1000 lines (and is a monopitch! F3). So, I could also translate 1000くらいの設定 as "around 1000 (oto) lines." However, I really really like that settei and settings look/sound similar. It's less accurate, technically, but I still think it works better.

すぐになめらかoverlap
sugi ni nameraka overlap
I'll easily have a smooth overlap.

Overlap is where one note fades into the one before it. It's smoother the better it is.

Text on Calogado's cape: *Performance may differ from person to person (※性能には個人差があります seinou ni wa kojinsa ga arimasu)

Calogado's wearing a cape, but they aren't the prince… once more, this is probably fine; Heki wears a witch outfit despite not being the sea witch.

今から私の言うことを繰り返してくださいね～！

This time, Calogado dresses like a butler, serving you a plate of oto.ini. Luckily I've already explained what an oto.ini is, so you can get this one!

Rest in peace, Ongentoro!

Rest in peace, Ongentoro! is kind of an Americanization here because 成仏 is "gaining enlightenment" like attaining nirvana and becoming a Buddha. However, in my defense, it also has a general meaning of "dying peacefully" i.e. resting in peace.

After telling Calogado to rest in peace, Heki throws salt at them. The bag is labeled 食用塩ミネラル (shokuyou shio mineraru) — "edible salt mineral." Salt famously wards off evil spirits.

もう墓まで同じよ運命共同体

mou haka made onaji yo unmeikyoudoutai

Well, until we're six feet under, it looks like we're in the same boat!

墓まで (haka made) is "until the grave" but that's not really natural, so I translated it as something less literal. And I could've said "until we die," but I wanted to include a reference to graves like the original verse does. Hence, "six feet under."

運命共同体 (unmeikyoudoutai) is an expression meaning to share a common destiny, or to be in the same boat. This uses the word 運命 (unmei, fate) and 共同体 (kyoudoutai, community). Heki is now in the UTAU community forever, because his voice has been stolen and put into .wav files. And now, it's been distributed to everyone with an internet connection.

Extra Translations

Video description

みんなもUTAUになろう！！！！！！！

歌　カロガド(連続音)、真宵ヘキ
https://avogado6.wixsite.com/calogado
多分カロガド(連続音)と真宵ヘキのデモソングです。

Let's all become UTAU too!!!!!!!

Singers: Calogado (VCV), Mayoi Heki
https://avogado6.wixsite.com/calogado
This is Calogado (VCV) and Mayoi Heki's demo song (kind of).

連続音(renzokuon) is the Japanese term for VCV. Literally "continuous sound." By the way, the term for CV is 単独音 (tandokuon). Literally "single sound."

Calogado has both a VCV and CV voicebank, but Mayoi Heki only has a VCV so that's why it's not specified here.

"What's a VCV voicebank?" you may ask, then, because I haven't explained this and the explanations you get when you look it up are shit.

Firstly, I'll explain what a CV voicebank is. CV (consonant-vowel) voicebanks are (usually) made by recording mora one at a time, so instead of ああんいあうあい.wav, you have あ.wav, ん.wav, etc. These are very easy to make, but the sound isn't as smooth as a VCV.

VCV (vowel-consonant-vowel) is smoother than CV since the vowel (or nasal ん) of the previous note is used for the start of the next note. For example, ohayo would be as [- o] [o は] [a よ]. In CV, this would just be [o] [ha] [yo].

Since you have to oto 7 different times for the same mora, VCV is more time-consuming. But it's all worth it for the nameraka overlap.

想定される質問

Questions I might get asked

Q. OREMOはMacだと起動できないので録音できません！
A. RecStarがあります。逃げるな。

Q. OREMO doesn't work on my Mac so I can't record anything!
A. There's RecStar. Don't run away.

Q. 連続音の録音は大変でできません！
A. 単独音やCVVC、または早いBPMの録音だと比較的楽です。逃げるな。

Q. It's way too hard to record a VCV so I can't do it!
A. There's CV and CVVC, and recording with a fast BPM isn't too difficult. Don't run away.

Surprisingly, CVVC is seem easier to record than VCV despite there being more letters in CVVC.

Q. 声が出せないのでできません！
A. 無生物音源ってのがあります。逃げるな。

Q. I'm unable to use my voice so I can't do it!
A. There are UTAU made from inanimate objects. Don't run away.

Q. 原音設定が難しくてできません！
A. その手の猛者がたくさんいらっしゃるので相談してみましょう。逃げるな。

Q. Otoing is too difficult so I can't do it!
A. You can consult a lot of people who are experts in that kind of thing. Don't run away.

原音設定 (genon settei) is what the English UTAU community refers to as otoing. Literally "fundamental tone settings." It's fun finding out how much Japanese UTAU terms differ from English ones LOL.

Q. パソコンを持ってないのでできません！
A. 有志の方がスマホでもUTAUを楽しめる環境を整えて下さっています。逃げるな。

Q. I don't have a PC so I can't do it!
A. Thanks to the work of volunteers, you can make an UTAU even from your phone. Don't run away.

With RecStar (Apple/Android), Laberu, and Gakuya, you can create an UTAU using only your phone. These UTAU are called "mobileloids."

Honestly, this is a bit difficult, so if you have access to a PC I would recommend using a PC instead.

Ongentoro Project Files

The song, along with all of its assets (ustx, MV, stem, etc.), are available for free on avogado6's UTAU website. This includes the music video's .psd file. So, let's check out the insides of Ongentoro.

"Good Boy Hands"

There's two subfolders in Calogado's folder called "good boy hand 1" and "good boy hand 2." (いいこいいこハンド, iiko iiko hando)

Yes, Calogado's petting Heki. I didn't move the hands; this is their default position. Petting Mayoi Heki.

Calogado Deleted Scene

There's a subfolder in Calogado's folder that shows a scrapped drawing. The folder's called 没 (botsu), meaning rejected (manuscript, etc.).

I find this expression absolutely adorable, like Calogado's trying to get a high-five that never comes. What actually ended up in the MV looks quite similar to this.
